title: Effect of Altitude on Gasoline Combustion Efficiency in Light-Duty Vehicles: Evidence from Andean Corridors (0–4000 m a.s.l.)
content: The reduction of air density with increasing altitude poses a persistent challenge for spark-ignition engines in light-duty vehicles, particularly in Andean countries where the vehicle fleet operates daily between sea level and over 4000 m a.s.l. This study quantified the effect of altitude on gasoline combustion efficiency and pollutant formation under real driving conditions, based on the analysis of 94263 second-by-second records collected over four years (2021–2025) from a fleet of ten light-duty Euro 2–5 vehicles (1000–2500 cm3) travelling along Andean and coastal corridors in Ecuador in the range 0m–4000m a.s.l. Instantaneous emissions were measured with a Brain Bee AGS-688 gas analyser with integrated pressure compensation; fuel consumption was obtained via OBD-II; and operational demand was characterised using the smoothed Vehicle Specific Power (PSVm10) grouped into six K-Means clusters. The ratios RCO=[CO]/[CO2] and RHC=[HC]/[CO2] are proposed as standardised combustion quality indicators, independent of engine displacement and dilution effects. Results show that RCO in the 3500–4000 m band exceeds the value in the 500–1000 m band by 7.5 times, and RHC by 18 times, evidencing progressive deterioration of combustion with altitude. Nitric oxide exhibited a non-linear “N”-pattern, with a local maximum at 2000–2500 m (212 ppm) and an absolute maximum at 3500–4000 m (613 ppm), linked to progressive EGR suppression and increased combustion chamber temperature. CO emission factors reached 6.42 g/km in the 2000–2500 m band, compared to 1.32 g/km in the coastal 500–1000 m band (4.9×). These results provide the first naturalistic evidence base at the Andean corridor scale for calibrating emission inventory models at high altitude.
